content: The DEFINE trial was a 76-week, global, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study designed to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of anacetrapib, a cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitor, when added to ongoing statin therapy in patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) or CHD risk-equivalent conditions. The primary objective of the trial was to assess both the therapeutic benefits and adverse effects of anacetrapib, either alone or in combination with statin therapy. The trial was registered under the identification number NCT00685776. Patients included in the study were required to be on statin therapy, with or without additional lipid-modifying therapy, since the conclusion of the baseline study and were expected to continue statin therapy throughout the trial. Exclusion criteria included a history of heart failure, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, or stroke within three months prior to screening, as well as uncontrolled hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, or liver disease. At 24 weeks, patients receiving anacetrapib demonstrated a significant reduction in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels, with LDL-C levels approximately halved from 81 mg/dL to 45 mg/dL. High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels increased from 41 mg/dL to 101 mg/dL. These changes were even more pronounced in patients with baseline HDL-C levels below 40 mg/dL, who experienced a 152% increase in HDL-C. Additionally, significant reductions in apolipoprotein B (ApoB), non-HDL cholesterol, lipoprotein(a), and triglycerides, as well as an increase in apolipoprotein A-I (ApoA-I), were observed at both 24 and 76 weeks. During the reversal phase of the study, 1,398 patients were enrolled. The reductions in LDL-C, non-HDL cholesterol, and ApoB, along with increases in HDL-C and ApoA-I, persisted during this phase for patients on anacetrapib, even though only trace concentrations of the medication were detected. These changes reached 50-60% of the values observed during the on-medication trial period. Adverse events associated with anacetrapib were not significantly different from those observed in the placebo group. Common adverse events in both groups included elevations in systolic and diastolic blood pressures, electrolyte disturbances, increased creatinine kinase levels, and myalgias. A small decrease in serum sodium levels was noted in patients on anacetrapib compared to placebo. In conclusion, anacetrapib was associated with a significant increase in HDL-C and a reduction in LDL-C, with a tolerable side effect profile. However, further clinical trials are necessary to confirm the potential cardiovascular benefits of increasing HDL-C levels in high-risk patients and to determine whether these changes translate into a reduction in adverse cardiovascular events.
